hints: Focus on what enthalpy of neutralisation really means, the energy change per mole of water formed, not per mole of acid or alkali.
Work out the heat released first using total mixture volume and temperature rise, then work out moles of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{NaOH}$ to find moles of water made.
Remember $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is diprotic, so check how many moles of $\text{H}^+$ react, then divide your heat energy by the moles of water to get kJ mol$^{-1}$ with a negative sign.
walkthrough:
**Find the heat energy released**

Think of the whole mixture getting warmer together. Total volume is $50 + 100 = 150 \text{ cm}^3$ and temperature rise is $29 - 20 = 9 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ (which is $9 \text{ K}$).

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$q = \text{volume} \times \text{specific heat capacity} \times \Delta T$$
$$q = 150 \times 4.2 \times 9 = 5670 \text{ J} = 5.67 \text{ kJ}$$

**Find moles of reactants and moles of water formed**

Now count particles. Both solutions are $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$n = c \times V$$
$$n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 1.0 \times \frac{50}{1000} = 0.050 \text{ mol}$$
$$n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.0 \times \frac{100}{1000} = 0.10 \text{ mol}$$

**Link to neutralisation equation**

The balanced equation shows why this mixture is exactly balanced:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$0.050$ mol of diprotic acid provides $0.10$ mol $\text{H}^+$, which exactly neutralises $0.10$ mol $\text{OH}^-$ to make $0.10$ mol of water.

**Calculate enthalpy per mole of water**

Enthalpy of neutralisation is heat released per $1$ mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ formed. The reaction is exothermic, so the sign is negative.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\Delta H_{neut} = -\frac{q}{n(\text{H}_2\text{O})}$$
$$\Delta H_{neut} = -\frac{5.67}{0.10} = -56.7 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

options.A: This is double the correct value. It comes from dividing $5.67$ kJ by $0.05$ mol of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ instead of $0.10$ mol of water. Remember $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ makes two moles of water per mole of acid.
options.B: This is correct. Total heat released is $5670$ J for $0.10$ mol of water formed, giving $-56.7$ kJ per mole of water, which matches the standard enthalpy of neutralisation for a strong acid and strong base.
options.C: This comes from dividing $5.67$ kJ by $0.15$ mol, the total moles of acid plus alkali added together. That has no chemical meaning. You must divide by moles of water actually formed.
options.D: This is far too small. It comes from using only one solution volume (e.g. $50 \text{ cm}^3$) instead of the total $150 \text{ cm}^3$ when calculating $q$. The heat warms the whole final mixture.
